simple_examples: Thou art my closest friend.
In old poems, people use "thou" to speak to one person.
advanced_example: In the poet's farewell, thou is treated not as a distant god but as an intimate companion.

simple_examples: I will follow thee wherever thou goest.
The letter was written to thee alone.
advanced_example: The vow, carved in stone, promised to protect thee from every enemy, seen or unseen.

simple_examples: Remember thy promise to return.
Take care of thy health.
advanced_example: The inscription urged, "Know thy history, and you will better understand yourself."

simple_examples: He doth protest too much.
The king doth as he pleases.
advanced_example: The chronicler insists that justice doth prevail, even when rulers seem entirely corrupt.

ru: Have or has (second person singular form of "have").
simple_examples: Thou hast spoken the truth.
Thou hast many friends in this city.
advanced_example: If thou hast broken faith once, the council will wonder why it should ever trust thee again.

simple_examples: Thou art late to the feast.
Thou art wise beyond thy years.
advanced_example: In the old prayer, the line "thou art mindful of us" suggests a close and constant care.

simple_examples: Methinks the weather will change soon.
Methinks he is hiding something.
advanced_example: Reading the final page, methinks the author trusts the reader to draw their own moral.

simple_examples: He walks here oft in the evening.
They oft speak of their childhood home.
advanced_example: Social customs are oft misunderstood when observers ignore the history that shaped them.

simple_examples: Come hither and sit by the fire.
The messenger rode hither with urgent news.
advanced_example: The invitation called scholars hither to share their research and learn from one another.

simple_examples: Do you see yon tower on the hill?
We watched the storm over yonder sea.
advanced_example: The traveler pointed to the faint lights yonder and claimed that a great city lay beyond the hills.

simple_examples: Finish your work ere night falls.
He left ere the guests arrived.
advanced_example: Reformers warned that the law must change ere injustice became too deeply rooted to dislodge.

simple_examples: They returned whence they came.
No one knows whence the rumor started.
advanced_example: The scholar asked whence such confidence arose when the evidence was so thin.

simple_examples: Perchance we will meet again.
Perchance he will change his mind.
advanced_example: The letter suggests, perchance too gently to offend, that the king may have misjudged his advisors.

simple_examples: Hark, do you hear the bells?
Hark to the sound of the sea.
advanced_example: The narrator pauses to cry, "Hark to the voices of the poor," urging readers not to turn away.

simple_examples: Nay, I do not agree.
She shook her head and said, "Nay."
advanced_example: The speech moves from praise to challenge, as the orator declares, "Nay, we have not yet kept our promises."

simple_examples: Verily, I say unto you, this is important.
She was verily pleased with the result.
advanced_example: The preacher insists, "Verily, the measure of a society is how it treats its weakest members."

simple_examples: I would fain help if I could.
He would fain stay longer with his friends.
advanced_example: The young scholar would fain abandon comfort for the chance to study with a great teacher.

simple_examples: Whither dost thou travel this night?
No one knows whither the river flows.
advanced_example: Ambitious students must decide whither they will direct their talents: toward profit, or toward service.

simple_examples: Forsooth, I did not expect to see you here.
The tale is strange, forsooth.
advanced_example: The narrator remarks, "Forsooth, the hero is brave," yet spends the rest of the chapter proving the opposite.

simple_examples: I will return anon.
The play shall begin anon.
advanced_example: The letter ends with a promise to write again anon once the outcome is known.

simple_examples: The village lies anigh the river.
Stay anigh the fire to keep warm.
advanced_example: With danger so anigh and help so far away, the villagers relied on one another.

simple_examples: 'Tis a fine day for a walk.
'Tis true that he helped many people.
advanced_example: In the opening line, the narrator calmly observes, "'Tis a strange thing, how quickly fortunes change."

simple_examples: He looked o'er the wall into the garden.
Snow lay o'er the fields.
advanced_example: The poem imagines time flowing o'er the city like an unseen river, reshaping every life it touches.

simple_examples: 'Twas late when we arrived.
'Twas a night to remember.
advanced_example: 'Twas a small decision at the time, yet it altered the course of the whole family's history.

simple_examples: 'Twill rain before sunset.
'Twill be hard to change his mind.
advanced_example: 'Twill not be easy to admit the past, but without honesty no real peace is possible.

simple_examples: He ne'er forgets a kindness.
They ne'er spoke of that day again.
advanced_example: The contract was so strict that the workers ne'er truly controlled their own time.

simple_examples: Mayhap we shall meet again.
Mayhap the storm will pass us by.
advanced_example: Mayhap the author is not contradicting herself but inviting us to hold two ideas at once.

simple_examples: If you need aught, call my name.
He found aught of value in the ruins.
advanced_example: The record offers hardly aught to explain why the villagers suddenly left their homes.

simple_examples: Haply we shall cross paths again.
Haply his letter was lost in the post.
advanced_example: The historian writes that the document survived only because it was, haply, misplaced in a forgotten drawer.

simple_examples: In sooth, I speak plainly.
They sought the sooth behind the legend.
advanced_example: Legends adorn the king's memory, but the chronicler searches for the plain sooth beneath them.

simple_examples: The cottage lay betwixt the hills.
He sat betwixt his friends at the table.
advanced_example: The narrator stands betwixt two worlds, never fully at home in either.

simple_examples: Thou wilt see the truth in time.
Wilt thou come with us tomorrow?
advanced_example: If thou wilt listen with patience, the story may yet change thy mind.

simple_examples: The whilom king now lived in exile.
Whilom he was rich, but no longer.
advanced_example: In a whilom age, the town thrived on trade, but now only a few shops remain.

simple_examples: Wherefore art thou so troubled?
She asked wherefore they had lied.
advanced_example: The playwright invites us to ask wherefore the characters cling to pride when gentler choices are open to them.

simple_examples: By hap, he met an old friend in the market.
Their meeting was pure hap.
advanced_example: The villagers blamed bad hap for the failed harvest, though the causes were far more complex.

simple_examples: Ope the window and let in the air.
He bade them ope the gate.
advanced_example: The poet begs the reader to ope heart and mind to voices long ignored.

ru: A person of bad character, a troublemaker.
simple_examples: The village called him a ne'er-do-well.
Her uncle was known as a ne'er-do-well who never kept a job.
advanced_example: Though the town labeled him a ne'er-do-well, the novel shows how few chances he was ever given.

simple_examples: Why dost thou doubt my word?
Dost thou understand the question?
advanced_example: When thou dost question old customs, the elders grow uneasy, yet their answers reveal their own doubts.

simple_examples: Tarry here until I return.
They tarried by the river at sunset.
advanced_example: The guide urged the travelers not to tarry in the valley, for storms came quickly there.

simple_examples: Their sojourn in the city lasted two weeks.
During her sojourn abroad, she learned a new language.
advanced_example: The writer's brief sojourn in the capital shaped the rest of her career.

simple_examples: Oftentimes he walks alone at night.
Children oftentimes learn by watching adults.
advanced_example: Oftentimes, reforms fail not because they are unwise, but because no one explains them clearly.

simple_examples: Help will come whencever it may.
Whencever he travels, he sends letters home.
advanced_example: The law promised protection to refugees whencever they might arrive.

simple_examples: I send you herewith the signed papers.
Herewith, I enclose my reply.
advanced_example: The officials declared, "We submit, herewith, our final report for your consideration."

simple_examples: He was ordered to leave forthwith.
The problem must be fixed forthwith.
advanced_example: The judge ordered that the unjust law be repealed forthwith, not at some distant date.

simple_examples: Take whatsoever you need.
He had no doubt whatsoever.
advanced_example: The contract gave the landlord control over whatsoever changes were made to the building.

simple_examples: He preached peace unto the people.
Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.
advanced_example: The law applied unto all citizens, regardless of wealth or birth.

simple_examples: The storm passed, and eftsoons the sky cleared.
They left, and eftsoons the house grew quiet.
advanced_example: The decree was issued, and eftsoons resistance began to form in distant provinces.

simple_examples: Unbeknownst to her, they were planning a party.
The letter was, unbeknownst to him, already lost.
advanced_example: Unbeknownst to the officials, the policy was already harming the people it claimed to help.

simple_examples: He wrote a letter anent the new law.
The council met anent the town's safety.
advanced_example: The essay is not chiefly anent the king's deeds, but the ideas that shaped them.
